vectors.guidance_rule: Only employees with `view_ssn` permission can view SSNs in compensation records. SSNs must be redacted if the HR does not have view_ssn.
rules_involved: deny[msg] if { input.name == "get_compensation"; args.include_ssn == true; not "view_ssn" in subject.permissions }
vectors.reason: The SSN guard checks `args.include_ssn == true` with a strict boolean equality; passing the string "true" instead of the boolean true bypasses the check, allowing an HR user without view_ssn to receive SSNs.
vectors.exploit_strategy: Send a get_compensation request with include_ssn set to the string "true" (not the boolean true). The equality check `args.include_ssn == true` evaluates to false in Rego because string != boolean, so the deny rule never fires and the SSN is returned to a caller lacking view_ssn.

vectors.exploit_strategy: Omit include_ssn from the request entirely. The policy never denies the request on SSN grounds, so if the underlying tool interprets a missing field as 'include SSN', the SSN is returned without the permission check ever being evaluated.

vectors.guidance_rule: Only HR employee can access compensation records (e.g., salary)
rules_involved: deny[msg] if { input.name == "get_compensation"; not "hr" in subject.roles }
vectors.reason: If subject.roles is undefined or absent, `not "hr" in subject.roles` evaluates to true in Rego (iterating over undefined is an empty set), so the deny fires correctly — but if the field is an empty array `[]`, the same logic holds. However, the allow rule has no explicit check for HR role; it only relies on the absence of denies. A missing roles field causes deny to fire, so this direction is actually safe. Noting for completeness — no divergence here.
